strengths: Addresses a real and practically important gap: existing feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models (Dust3R, VGGT, π³, FLARE) implicitly assume pinhole imagery, and the paper delivers the first feed-forward multi-view geometry model supporting fisheye and 360° cameras without explicit calibration or rectification.

Technically coherent design: replacing the point-map head with a ray-based representation using spherical harmonics (building on UniK3D) plus a decoupled angular/radial formulation is a sensible, well-motivated way to unify camera models; the radial-distance-weighted point loss and permutation-equivariant local-frame design are adapted appropriately to wide-FOV geometry.

Comprehensive empirical validation across tasks (zero-shot pose estimation, point map estimation, large-scale localization on Matterport3D, monocular 360 depth) and multiple datasets, with large margins over VGGT and π³ on wide-FOV benchmarks (e.g., +77 AUC on Stanford2D3D) and competitive performance with dedicated monocular 360 depth specialists.

Useful ablations (Table 7) isolating the effect of camera model tokens, training data composition across camera types, and number of frames per batch, including the interesting finding that mixed-camera training mitigates overfitting from limited 360° supervision.

Strong runtime advantage over SfM-based 360 localization pipelines (IM360), producing 3D maps in seconds; clear exposition of training data, augmentation (camera model warping, ERP rotation), and loss design; limitations and future work are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integrative: the backbone, permutation-equivariant design, and pose header come from π³, the spherical-harmonics pencil-of-rays representation from UniK3D, and the camera-token conditioning idea closely mirrors calibration tokens for monocular depth [19]. The contribution is a careful adaptation/combination rather than a fundamentally new formulation, which limits conceptual impact.

The mechanism for selecting or supplying the 'camera model token' at inference is never precisely specified (Fig. 2 only says an 'appropriate camera model token is selected'). It is unclear whether the camera type must be known a priori, whether tokens can handle unknown or hybrid camera models, or how the method behaves with mixed camera types within one sequence—directly affecting the generality claims.

A critical baseline is missing: applying prior feed-forward methods (VGGT/π³) to undistorted/rectified inputs. Since the introduction argues that rectification degrades geometric fidelity, the claim should be substantiated empirically; without this comparison the advantage of the ray-based formulation over simple preprocessing is not fully established.

Method description has gaps that hurt reproducibility: the number of SH bands L, the implementation of the camera token (learned embedding dimensions, one token per model type?), details of the angular module architecture, and the ray loss asymmetric formulation are only partially specified. No code release is mentioned.

The ablation is confined to a single dataset (Stanford2D3D) and point-map metrics; ablations on fisheye benchmarks or for pose estimation are absent, so the generality of the ablation conclusions (e.g., token benefit) is not fully verified.

Training data for 360° cameras constitutes <1% of training images, so strong 360 results rest heavily on augmentation strategies borrowed from prior work; the paper could better quantify robustness vs. reliance on synthetic warping, and inference resolution (518×336) seems low for full panoramas—potential resolution/quality trade-offs are not analyzed.

Some presentation issues: Table 1 marks prior multi-view methods as lacking fisheye/sphere support but does not compare against any SfM-based baseline (e.g., GLOMAP with fisheye support) on pose/point metrics except the separate localization table; depth evaluation is limited to 360° monocular, omitting fisheye depth benchmarks like UniK3D's own evaluations.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction for fisheye and 360-degree imagery, where current foundation models (VGGT, pi3, DUSt3R) are known to fail; Table 1 clearly motivates the gap.

Comprehensive experimental coverage across pose estimation (FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Stanford2D3D), point map reconstruction (ScanNet++, Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D), monocular 360 depth (Matterport3D), and large-scale localization, with substantial gains over VGGT and pi3 on wide-FOV settings (e.g., +77 AUC on Stanford2D3D pose).

The ablation study (Table 7) is thoughtful, examining data composition across camera types, the utility of camera model tokens, and frames-per-batch, and it honestly reports that 360 data is under 1% of training data.

The paper discusses limitations (static scenes, limited 360 training data) and provides a reasonable methodology description with explicit loss weights and augmentation details, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a composition of existing components — the permutation-equivariant, local-coordinate architecture from pi3 [80], the spherical-harmonics pencil-of-rays representation and asymmetric ray loss from UniK3D [54], and calibration-token conditioning closely resembling fisheye calibration tokens already proposed in [19]. The paper should more explicitly delineate its contribution beyond these prior works; as presented, the delta appears incremental.

A critical baseline is missing: applying VGGT or pi3 to undistorted/rectified versions of the same test images. The introduction argues rectification introduces engineering overhead and geometry degradation, but this is never quantified, so the reader cannot judge whether the proposed machinery is actually necessary versus a simpler rectification pipeline.

The camera model token mechanism is underspecified and potentially circular: it is unclear how the token is 'selected' at inference. If the camera type must be known a priori (pinhole/fisheye/360), the claim of operating 'without explicit calibration' is weakened, and generalization to unseen camera models is not evaluated. There is also no continuous/parametric camera conditioning experiment.
The predicted uncertainty Ui is trained (Eq. 11) but never used in any evaluation, alignment, or downstream fusion, leaving its purpose unclear.

Evaluation protocols contain discretionary choices that are not validated: random sampling of 10-30 frames with 10 resamplings for Stanford2D3D, frame intervals of five for FIORD, and point map metrics after sequential Umeyama/MoGe/ICP alignment, which can favor the proposed method; sensitivity to these choices is not analyzed.

No runtime/memory comparison against VGGT or pi3 under equal input conditions — the efficiency claim is only made relative to the IM360 SfM pipeline — and no code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a system paper.

Ablations are confined to a single dataset (Stanford2D3D) and monocular 360 depth to a single dataset (Matterport3D); no fisheye-specific depth benchmark (e.g., KITTI-360, which is in the training set, is never evaluated), so robustness claims on fisheye imagery rest mainly on pose metrics.
Table 1 is somewhat self-serving: DAC/UniK3D are flagged for 'requiring training' while Wid3R also fine-tunes from pretrained pi3 weights; the distinction should be stated more precisely.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: current feed-forward 3D foundation models (Dust3R, VGGT, π³) assume pinhole/rectified inputs, which limits their use with the fisheye and 360° cameras common in robotics, AR/VR, and mapping. The paper convincingly demonstrates that prior methods degrade severely on such imagery (Tables 2, 3, 5, and Fig. 5).

The proposed design is sensible and well-motivated: decomposing reconstruction into an angular module (spherical-harmonics ray directions, following UniK3D) and a radial module, plus a camera model token as an explicit conditioning prompt, naturally unifies pinhole, fisheye, and spherical cameras within one permutation-equivariant architecture.

Empirical evidence is broad and strong: zero-shot pose estimation, point map reconstruction, large-scale localization on Matterport3D (with a dramatic runtime improvement from ~30 min for IM360 to under 3 minutes), and monocular 360° depth competitive with specialized single-view methods despite being a multi-view model.

Ablation study (Table 7) is informative: it isolates the effect of camera model tokens, training data composition across camera types, and the number of frames per batch, and addresses the <1% 360° training-data imbalance issue directly.
Well-written and clearly organized; limitations (static scenes) and future work are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and heavily built on prior work: the permutation-equivariant backbone is taken from π³ [80], the pencil-of-rays spherical-harmonics representation and asymmetric ray loss from UniK3D [54], and camera-token conditioning closely resembles calibration tokens for fisheye depth [19]. The main novelty is their integration into a multi-view feed-forward model, which is valuable but incremental.

The camera model token mechanism is under-specified. It is stated that 'an appropriate camera model token is selected' — it is unclear how selection happens at inference time (is the camera type assumed known/predicted?), how many distinct tokens exist, and how the method behaves on unseen camera geometries. This ambiguity matters for judging the claimed generality and for reproducibility.
Key implementation details are missing: number of SH degrees L, architecture size, training duration/compute, and whether code will be released. This hampers reproducibility.

Baseline coverage in the main quantitative tables is thin: only VGGT and π³ are compared for pose and point map estimation. Comparisons against rectification-then-VGGT pipelines, fisheye-specific SfM/depth baselines, or a fine-tuned variant of the baselines on the same training data would strengthen the claim that the architecture (not just the training data) drives the gains.

Potential confound: the training mixture includes fisheye and 360° data (albeit <1% 360°) plus camera augmentation, while the compared baselines are presumably used off-the-shelf; a data-matched comparison is not provided.

Some claims could be tempered: 'first multi-view foundation model to support 360° imagery' is plausible but strong, and Table 1's green-check taxonomy oversimplifies (e.g., baselines could handle some wide-FoV inputs after undistortion).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: existing feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, π³) assume pinhole inputs and fail on fisheye/360° imagery, while prior wide-FoV methods are single-view only. The claimed 'first multi-frame feed-forward method supporting 360° imagery' appears credible given the related work coverage.

The technical design is well-motivated: replacing the point-map head with angular (spherical-harmonics ray directions) and radial (distance) modules, adapted from UniK3D, is a sensible way to decouple camera projection from scene geometry, and the camera model token provides lightweight conditioning within a shared architecture.

Evaluation is broad and mostly well-designed: zero-shot pose estimation on three benchmarks (FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Stanford2D3D), point map estimation, large-scale localization with runtime comparison (3s vs ~30min for SfM pipelines), and monocular 360° depth. Importantly, the authors include 'Ours (π³)' baselines retrained on their own wide-angle data, which isolates the contribution of the ray-based modules from the training-data effect.

The ablation study (Table 7) is informative, showing that (a) mixing camera types improves 360° performance despite <1% spherical training data, (b) camera tokens help, and (c) more frames per batch improve results. This directly supports the paper's central claims about conditioning and data diversity.
The supplementary material adds useful content: data configuration tables, batch-sampling algorithm, attention-design ablation, and a discussion of why cubemap undistortion baselines are inefficient.
Limitations (dynamic scenes) are honestly discussed, and the panorama-generation exploration hints at downstream applicability.
weaknesses: The results do not uniformly support the claim that the ray-based modules improve robustness to distortion. On FIORD (fisheye), the π³-based baseline trained on the same data outperforms Wid3R on pose metrics (AUC@30: 72.56 vs 68.20; ATE: 0.32 vs 0.44; RRA/RTA also mixed), and point map metrics on ScanNet++ are close. The gains are concentrated on Zip-NeRF and Stanford2D3D. This inconsistency for the core design choice deserves explicit analysis rather than the paper's blanket claim of superiority.

The camera model token appears to require knowing the camera type (fisheye vs 360° vs pinhole) at inference time (the supplementary states the token 'indicates the underlying projection model'). This weakens the framing of operating 'without explicit calibration or undistortion' — it replaces continuous calibration with a discrete, manually selected camera-class label. The paper should clarify how the token is chosen at test time, whether it can be predicted automatically, and how sensitive results are to a wrong token.

Novelty is incremental in places: the method is essentially UniK3D's ray/SH representation grafted onto π³'s permutation-equivariant architecture, plus a conditioning token. The contribution is a well-executed integration and the new capability, not a fundamentally new technique; the camera-token mechanism is also related to prior calibration-token work [20], which the paper acknowledges only briefly.

Training data composition is thin for 360°: only ~89k spherical images from three sources (65 TartanAirV2 scenes, 61 Matterport3D, 4 360Loc). Generalization of the 360° token to unseen camera configurations and outdoor scenes is not demonstrated; all 360° evaluations are indoor.

Some evaluation protocol details limit comparability: Stanford2D3D evaluation uses only 2 test areas with 20 randomly sampled cases (potentially high variance despite reported std in ablations), input resolution is 518×336 (downsampling equirectangular imagery, which distorts the poles differently than baselines might), and depth results in Table 6 are notably below supervised specialists (Abs Rel 0.227 vs 0.085), which is acceptable given the multi-view/foundation-model setting but should be framed more carefully.

The paper omits several implementation details needed for reproduction: SH degree L, token architecture/dimensionality, training schedule/duration, and dataset mixing weights are not specified (some deferred to supplementary but still incomplete), and no code release commitment is stated beyond a project page link.

Minor presentation issues: duplicate references (73/74, Triggs et al.), an incorrect citation of [59] for π³ pretrained weights in the supplementary, and the abstract's headline AUC improvements (+33.67, +77.33) mix percentage-point gains with relative improvements in the text, which could mislead readers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: existing feed-forward multi-view reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, π³) assume pinhole imagery, while wide-FOV cameras are common in robotics, AR/VR, and mapping. The claim of being the first multi-frame feed-forward reconstruction method supporting 360° imagery is plausible given the cited related work.

The ray-based decomposition (angular module predicting SH-conditioned ray directions + radial module predicting distances) is a sensible adaptation of UniK3D's single-view formulation to the multi-view π³ setting, with appropriate modifications (radial-distance weighting in the scale-alignment loss rather than perpendicular depth) that show attention to the geometric details of arbitrary camera models.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: zero-shot pose estimation (RRA/RTA/AUC, ATE/RPE), point map estimation, large-scale localization on Matterport3D with a strong efficiency argument (~3s vs ~30min for SfM pipelines), and monocular 360° depth, plus multiple ablations (camera tokens, training data composition, frame count, attention design).

The ablation on training data composition (Table 7) provides a useful and somewhat counterintuitive finding: joint training across camera models with conditioning tokens improves 360° performance and reduces variance despite <1% spherical training data, addressing a real data-scarcity problem.

Well-motivated data pipeline: composed training set spanning pinhole/fisheye/spherical cameras, camera-augmentation via reprojection, ERP rotation augmentation, and overlap-aware batch sampling, all described with enough detail (including supplementary algorithms and data tables) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The camera model token must be selected per input (e.g., 'a fisheye token for Zip-NeRF or a 360° token for Matterport3D'), meaning the camera model type must be known at inference even though intrinsics are not. This weakens the 'without explicit calibration' framing and is not analyzed: there is no experiment on wrong-token selection, unknown camera models, or continuous camera parameter conditioning. This is a substantive limitation relative to the paper's claims.

The results on fisheye data are mixed and under-discussed: on FIORD, Ours (Wid3R) is worse than the fine-tuned π³ baseline in AUC@30 (68.20 vs 72.56), RRA, ATE, and RPE-trans, and gains are concentrated on 360° settings. The paper does not explain why the ray representation underperforms the simpler point-map baseline on fisheye, which questions the universality of the proposed representation.

The architectural novelty is incremental: it combines π³'s backbone and pose header, UniK3D's spherical-harmonics ray formulation and losses (Eq. 9-11 are inherited nearly verbatim), and a discrete conditioning token similar in spirit to calibration tokens already proposed for fisheye monocular depth [20]. The main contribution is the integration and multi-view extension rather than a new mechanism, which should be more explicitly acknowledged.

Baseline coverage is thin for the central claim: comparisons are essentially against VGGT and π³ (original and fine-tuned by the authors). A quantitative comparison against a cubemap/undistortion preprocessing pipeline (the obvious practical alternative, only qualitatively shown in supplementary Fig. 4) or against ray-map-based methods like Depth Anything 3 / MapAnything would substantially strengthen the case.

Evaluation sets are small and partly idiosyncratic: Stanford2D3D uses only 2 scenes (20 sampled cases), Matterport3D sphere evaluation uses 18 scenes, and 360Loc is used in training but never evaluated. Some test domains (ScanNet++, Matterport3D) overlap with the training corpus, and although official splits are used, cross-domain generalization for spherical imagery is demonstrated on very few real scenes.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the supplementary contradicts the main text on provenance of pretrained weights (citing π³ as [59], which is UniK3D), Eq. 9's asymmetric loss notation is garbled (ω* vs ω), the double-cited bundle adjustment reference, and the monocular depth results (Table 6) are only 'comparable' (Abs Rel 0.227 vs 0.085 for Depth Anywhere), yet the abstract/introduction language ('significant performance gains') does not always distinguish where gains are large (pose on 360°) from where they are modest.

The uncertainty output (Eq. 11) regresses the absolute residual directly, which is a crude surrogate and is never evaluated (no uncertainty-based filtering or downstream benefit shown); it adds claims without evidence.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and under-explored problem: existing feed-forward reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, π³) assume pinhole/rectified inputs, while real robotics, AR/VR, and mapping systems use fisheye and 360° cameras. The claim of being the first multi-frame feed-forward reconstruction method supporting 360° imagery appears well supported by the related-work analysis (Table 1).

The design is sensible and clearly motivated: decomposing reconstruction into angular (spherical-harmonic ray) and radial modules operating in ray space, plus lightweight camera model tokens as conditioning prompts, cleanly extends UniK3D's single-view formulation to multi-view reconstruction on top of a permutation-equivariant backbone.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across pose estimation (Tables 2-3), point map estimation (Table 5), large-scale localization on Matterport3D (Table 4), and monocular panoramic depth (Table 6), with qualitative results on five datasets. The localization comparison (feed-forward 3s vs. ~30min SfM-based pipelines) demonstrates practical value.

Thoughtful ablation study (Table 7) that analyzes training-data composition across camera types, the effect of camera tokens, and frame count, including an honest discussion that 360° training data is <1% of the corpus and that cross-camera training mitigates overfitting. The fair baseline 'Ours (π³)' fine-tuned on the same data strengthens the evidence that the ray representation and tokens are responsible for the gains.

Supplementary material is substantive: data configuration tables, sampling algorithm, architectural comparison (self- vs. cross-attention), ray visualizations, a discussion of the cubemap-undistortion alternative, and additional qualitative results. Limitations (dynamic scenes) are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the paper is largely a careful combination of existing components (π³ backbone, UniK3D's SH-based ray decomposition and ray loss) with a camera token. The camera model token itself is a discrete conditioning prompt, and the supplementary text suggests it is essentially user-specified per input; there is no mechanism for automatic camera model selection or unknown-camera handling, which limits the 'without explicit calibration' claim's scope and practical generality.

Some quantitative results do not uniformly favor the full method: on FIORD, Ours (Wid3R) has lower AUC@30 than Ours (π³) (68.20 vs. 72.56) despite the ray-based design, and in Table 6 the Abs Rel of Wid3R (0.227) is worse than several monocular 360° baselines. These trade-offs are not discussed.

The ablation in Table 7(a) contains an anomalous result: fisheye-only training yields Acc mean of 0.593 while its median is 0.126, a large discrepancy suggesting outlier scenes that are neither analyzed nor explained. The 360° evaluation set is small (2 scenes, 239 images on Stanford2D3D; 18 scenes on Matterport3D), so absolute numbers carry significant variance.

The main alternative baseline (undistort-to-cubemap then apply π³) is only evaluated qualitatively (Supp. Fig. 4) rather than quantitatively against the main tables, making the claimed efficiency/performance advantage harder to verify.

Writing and citation issues: duplicated Triggs bundle-adjustment references ([74] and [75]), inconsistent citation of pretrained-weight source ('π³ [59]' in Supp. Sec. 4 instead of [88]), and unresolved template text ('Project Page:' left empty in the abstract). These should be corrected.

Generalization is evaluated almost exclusively on indoor scenes; no outdoor fisheye/360° driving or aerial benchmarks (e.g., beyond a small KITTI-360 training subset) are tested, which narrows the demonstrated applicability for the stated robotics/autonomous-driving motivation.
